message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
You'll be fine. Here's everything in order.

## What "lippage" means

**Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it**, so you get a little ridge you can feel with your fingers or catch with a sock. It looks shoddy, especially when light shines across the floor, and it can be a trip or chip risk.

It's a particular risk with **30 × 60 cm tiles**, because long tiles are often very slightly bowed in the middle. Two things help:

- **Don't offset the rows by half a tile.** If you lay them in a staggered brick pattern, offset by **a third or less**. A half-offset puts the high middle of one tile against the low end of the next.
- **Use a tile levelling clip system.** These are cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull adjacent edges flush while the adhesive sets, and they're a big help for beginners.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for a **mid-grey, one or two shades darker than the tile**. It blends in, and it won't show dirt the way white or very pale grout does. Bathroom floor grout darkens with grime quickly.

For extra protection, look for a grout labelled stain-resistant or water-repellent, or apply a grout sealer once it has cured. Epoxy grout resists stains best, but it's harder for a first-timer to work with.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first.** The toilet should sit on the finished tiles. It looks neater, you avoid fiddly cuts around the base of the pan, and the toilet can be taken out later without disturbing the tiles. Just check that the waste pipe will still line up at the new floor height.

## How many boxes?

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 m × 1.8 m | 4.32 m² |
| Area of one tile | 0.3 m × 0.6 m | 0.18 m² |
| Tiles needed | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 | 24 tiles |
| Plus 10% | 24 × 1.1 = 26.4 | **27 tiles** |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4 | **4 boxes** (32 tiles) |

**Buy 4 boxes.** Three boxes gives exactly 24 tiles with no margin, which is too risky with cuts around the toilet, the doorway, and walls that are rarely perfectly square. The extra will cover a broken tile or a botched cut, and a couple of spares are worth keeping for future repairs. Check that all four boxes have the **same batch number**, since shades can vary slightly between batches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there may be some noise for a few hours. I'll try to keep it to sensible times and get it done as quickly as I can.
>
> Thanks so much for your patience, especially with the skip on the drive these past two weeks. It should be gone soon!
>
> Best wishes,
> [Your name], number [X]

## Three tips for a first-timer

1. **Prepare the subfloor properly.** It needs to be solid, flat, clean and dry before any tile goes down. Fill dips, screw down any flexing boards, or overlay timber floors with tile backer board, and prime if the adhesive maker says to. Most tiling problems come from the subfloor, not the tiles.
2. **Dry-lay before you mix anything.** Lay the tiles out loose with spacers to plan the pattern. You're aiming to avoid thin slivers at the doorway and other visible edges, so start from a line that gives balanced cuts rather than from the wall. Leave a small expansion gap of about 5 mm around the edges, which the skirting will hide.
3. **Work in small sections and check as you go.** Mix small batches of adhesive and spread only about a square metre at a time. With large tiles, also butter the back of each tile with a thin layer for full contact. Press tiles down with a slight twist, then check each one with a spirit level against its neighbours before the adhesive sets. You can correct mistakes for a few minutes, but not the next day.

Also buy knee pads. The videos never mention them, but your knees will notice.

Good luck. With careful prep and patience, your first floor should turn out well.
